items.title: feat: multi-agent A2A — sessions_list/history/send/spawn tools

labels.name: comp/agent
labels.description: Core agent runtime: loop, agent_init, prompt builder, context-compression, responses endpoint

items.body:
## Background

OpenClaw implements **Agent-to-Agent (A2A) communication** via session tools:

- `sessions_list` — discover active sessions and their metadata
- `sessions_history` — fetch transcript logs for any session  
- `sessions_send` — message another session with optional reply-back
- `sessions_spawn` — spawn a new sub-agent session with configurable model, workspace

This enables coordination: one agent can delegate to another, check status of other agents, share context between agents.

Hermes Agent has `delegate_task` for spawning sub-agents, but:
- No `sessions_list` to discover active sessions
- No `sessions_history` to fetch another session's transcript
- No `sessions_send` to message a running agent
- Sessions are not persistent/addressable by ID

## Proposal

Add A2A session tools:

1. **sessions_list**: Returns all active sessions with metadata (platform, model, last activity)
2. **sessions_history**: Fetch messages from a specific session by ID
3. **sessions_send**: Send a message to another active session; receive a reply
4. **sessions_spawn** (already exists as `delegate_task`, but could be enhanced with persistence)

## References

- OpenClaw: `docs/concepts/session-tool`

OpenClaw has **dedicated Chrome/Chromium browser control** via CDP:
- Opens a managed Chrome/Chromium instance with distinct profiles
- Full page snapshots, element clicking, form filling, uploads
- Multiple concurrent browser sessions with unique profiles

- Require Browserbase account for browser automation
- No local CDP control (can't directly drive a browser on the host)

Add optional local CDP browser control:

1. **Local CDP mode**: Launch a local Chrome/Chromium in headless mode
2. **Tool schema**: `browser_snapshot`, `browser_click`, `browser_type`, `browser_navigate` (already partially exist via Browserbase)
3. **Profile support**: Per-session browser profiles (like OpenClaw's `browser.profiles`)
4. **Fallback**: If local CDP fails or is not configured, fall back to Browserbase or web search
5. **Config**: `browser.enabled`, `browser.color`, `browser.profile` in `config.yaml`

items.title: [Hindsight] Add reference launchd plist for local_embedded daemon (macOS auto-restart)
items.body:
## Motivation

The `hindsight` memory plugin in `local_embedded` mode runs a background daemon that:

1. Auto-stops after 5 min of idle (`HINDSIGHT_EMBED_DAEMON_IDLE_TIMEOUT`, default 300)
2. Occasionally crashes on macOS (see related issue re: MPS/embeddings)
3. Does not restart automatically — `_get_client()` caches the client without health checking (Issue #7149, PR #7435 in progress)

For users running Hermes interactively over multi-hour or multi-day sessions, manually re-running `hindsight-embed -p <profile> daemon start` is a recurring paper cut.

## Proposal

Ship a reference launchd plist under `plugins/memory/hindsight/contrib/launchd/com.hindsight.embed.<profile>.plist.template` that users can `envsubst` and `launchctl load`.

Optionally add a CLI helper:

```bash
hermes memory autostart enable   # generates + loads plist
hermes memory autostart disable  # unloads + removes plist
```

## Working reference (tested on macOS 26.x Apple Silicon)

```xml
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
    <key>Label</key>
    <string>com.hindsight.embed.hermes</string>
    <key>ProgramArguments</key>
    <array>
        <string>${HERMES_VENV}/bin/hindsight-embed</string>
        <string>-p</string>
        <string>hermes</string>
        <string>daemon</string>
        <string>start</string>
    </array>
    <key>EnvironmentVariables</key>
    <dict>
        <key>PATH</key>
        <string>${HERMES_VENV}/bin:/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin:/bin</string>
    </dict>
    <key>RunAtLoad</key><true/>
    <key>KeepAlive</key>
    <dict>
        <key>SuccessfulExit</key><false/>
        <key>NetworkState</key><true/>
    </dict>
    <key>ThrottleInterval</key><integer>30</integer>
    <key>StandardOutPath</key><string>${HOME}/.hermes/logs/hindsight-launchd.out</string>
    <key>StandardErrorPath</key><string>${HOME}/.hermes/logs/hindsight-launchd.err</string>
    <key>WorkingDirectory</key><string>${HOME}</string>
</dict>
</plist>
```

Key flags:
- `KeepAlive.SuccessfulExit: false` — restart unless daemon exits cleanly
- `KeepAlive.NetworkState: true` — only run when network up (avoids cold-boot races, related to #5729)
- `ThrottleInterval: 30` — avoid restart loops if daemon is broken

## Equivalent for Linux (separate ask)

If accepted, a `systemd --user` unit template would round out cross-platform coverage, parallel to the existing `hermes gateway install` story.

## Related issues

- #7149 (daemon idle timeout, no client-side health check)
- #4820 (launchctl deprecated commands — same plist conventions apply)
- #6631 (gateway restart silent failure — same root concern: services dying unnoticed)

items.title: [Proposal] Formalize & Scale the Plugin System: Official Core Plugins + Third-Party Source Submission → Centralized Build & Distribution (to handle 2.4K+ PR volume)
items.body:
Hi @NousResearch team,
First of all, huge congratulations — Hermes Agent has become an absolute powerhouse (73k+ stars, extremely active development, and v0.8.0 just dropped). The self-improving agent loop, skills system, MCP, and the already-existing PluginManager + registry architecture are genuinely impressive.
However, the current contribution volume is now at a scale that the monorepo approach is struggling to handle:

2,329 open PRs and 4,467 closed PRs (as of April 2026)
This is an incredible sign of community enthusiasm, but it also creates massive review pressure on the core team, long merge queues, and makes it harder for users to discover and use new features quickly.

Proposal: Evolve the current plugin architecture into a true plugin ecosystem with two tiers

Core Plugins (officially maintained by NousResearch)
Kept in the main repo under plugins/core/ (or similar).
Cover the foundational, high-security, high-performance pieces (memory providers, context engines, official LLM adapters, official communication platforms, built-in toolsets, etc.).
These continue to follow the existing PluginManager, registry pattern, and skills system you already have.

Community / Extended Plugins (third-party contributed)
Third-party developers submit source code only (Python package + manifest) to a dedicated plugin submission endpoint / GitHub repository / web UI.
A centralized build & validation pipeline (running in a secure, isolated environment) compiles the plugin into a signed, versioned artifact (e.g. wheel, Nix package, or Docker layer).
The built plugin is then published to a public plugin registry (e.g. plugins.hermes-agent.nousresearch.com or a simple index on agentskills.io).
Users can install them with one command:Bashhermes plugin install community:telegram-enterprise
hermes plugin install llm:deepseek-r1-custom
This keeps the main hermes-agent repository lean while still giving the community a safe, official way to contribute and distribute extensions.


High-value examples that would benefit immediately

Additional communication platforms (Enterprise WeChat, Line, Rocket.Chat, custom IRC, etc.)
New LLM providers / custom endpoints (especially regional or specialized models)
Niche toolsets and memory backends that don’t need to live in the core
Experimental features that users want to try without waiting for core review

Benefits

Dramatically reduces PR noise in the main repo
Faster iteration for contributors (no more waiting months for review)
Safer distribution (official build pipeline can run security scans, tests, and signing)
Better discoverability and versioning for users
Scales the “agent that grows with you” philosophy to the plugin ecosystem itself

This is a natural evolution of the excellent modularity you already built (PluginManager, skills registry, provider resolution, gateway/platforms/, etc.). It would turn the current “2.4K PR firehose” into a healthy, sustainable open-source ecosystem.

What do you think? Would love to hear the team’s thoughts on making this the next big architectural step for Hermes Agent.
Thanks again for the amazing project!
(Your work is genuinely pushing the frontier of open-source agents.)

items.title: [Bug]: TTS truncates at first newline — Kokoro and potentially other backends
items.body:
## Description

Some TTS backends (confirmed: Kokoro/StyleTTS2 via OpenAI-compatible API) silently truncate text at the first `\n` character, causing only the first line of a multi-paragraph response to be spoken aloud.

The current `_strip_markdown_for_tts()` function strips markdown formatting but **preserves newlines** — which is correct for backends like Edge TTS that treat newlines as pauses, but breaks backends that truncate.

Additionally, emoji characters are not stripped and cause unnatural speech output across all TTS providers.

## Evidence

Controlled tests against Kokoro TTS (`/v1/audio/speech` endpoint):

| Input | Audio size | Result |
|-------|-----------|--------|
| `"Hello, I am your assistant."` (single line) | 205,244 bytes | Spoken correctly |
| `"Hello.\nSecond line.\nThird."` (with newlines) | 205,244 bytes | **Only first line spoken** |
| `"Hello. Second line. Third."` (newlines replaced with spaces) | 729,644 bytes | All text spoken |

The Kokoro API returns HTTP 200 in all cases — no error, just silent truncation.

## Proposed Fix

Add `_preprocess_tts_text()` that layers on top of `_strip_markdown_for_tts()`:

1. **Strip emojis** — Unicode emoji ranges (emoticons, symbols, pictographs, etc.)
2. **Strip table/box-drawing characters** — `|`, `─`, etc.
3. **Strip MEDIA: tags** — injected by the tool pipeline
4. **Convert newlines to sentence breaks** — `\n\n` to `. `, `\n` to ` `
5. **Collapse whitespace**

Newline stripping should be **configurable** via `tts.strip_newlines` (default: `true`) since some backends handle newlines correctly as pauses.

### Voice-mode system prompt

When `event.message_type == MessageType.VOICE`, inject guidance into the system prompt:
> "The user is speaking via voice and your response will be converted to live speech. Keep your response concise (1-3 sentences). Do not use emojis or special characters."

This reduces the need for heavy post-processing and produces more natural voice conversations.

## Related

- PR #8205 by @kas-cor — overlapping work on TTS text preprocessing with localized emoji speech. The emoji range approach in this fix is inspired by that PR.

## Environment

- TTS backend: Kokoro (StyleTTS2) via vLLM OpenAI-compatible endpoint
- Also affects: any TTS backend that does not handle `\n` in input text
- Hermes Agent: latest main

Description:

When running hermes gateway install --system on Amazon Linux 2023, the generated systemd service file uses the system Python (/usr/bin/python3.11) in the ExecStart line instead of the venv Python (~/.hermes/hermes-agent/venv/bin/python3).

This causes the service to crash immediately with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'yaml' because the system Python doesn't have Hermes dependencies installed.

Environment:

- Hermes Agent v0.8.0 (v2026.4.8)
- Amazon Linux 2023 (EC2 t2.large)
- Python 3.11 installed via sudo dnf install python3.11
- Using a named profile

Steps to reproduce:

1. Install Hermes on AL2023
2. Create a profile: hermes profile create mybot --clone
3. Install as system service: sudo env "PATH=$PATH" HERMES_HOME=/home/ec2-user/.hermes/profiles/mybot hermes gateway install --system
4. Start the service: sudo systemctl start hermes-gateway-mybot
5. Service crashes with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'yaml'

Expected: ExecStart should use /home/ec2-user/.hermes/hermes-agent/venv/bin/python3

Actual: ExecStart uses /usr/bin/python3.11

Workaround:

sudo sed -i 's|ExecStart=/usr/bin/python3.11|ExecStart=/home/ec2-user/.hermes/hermes-agent/venv/bin/python3|' /etc/systemd/system/hermes-gateway-mybot.service
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart hermes-gateway-mybot

## Why this issue exists
This is a user-outcome-first consolidation of open issues. It keeps only must-have capabilities that users need to reliably get value from Hermes.

## Selection criteria (strict)
- Blocks core user journey (send request -> get correct result -> deliver response)
- Affects many users/platforms or causes data/security risk

items.title: Gateway can immediately timeout fresh messages when cached agent carries stale activity timestamp
items.body:
## Summary
Gateway inactivity timeout can fire immediately on a fresh inbound message when the gateway reuses a cached `AIAgent` whose activity timestamp is stale from the previous turn.

## User-visible symptom
A user sends a new message after the session has been idle for a while and, within a few seconds, gets:

- `⚠️ No activity for 15 min...`
- `⏱️ Agent inactive for 30 min — no tool calls or API responses.`

Even though the new turn just started.

## Observed evidence
Affected session type: cached Telegram DM session

Relevant log sequence:

- `07:36:19` prior turn finished with `api_calls=21`
- `09:09:33` new inbound Telegram message arrived
- `09:09:38` gateway logged:
  - `Agent idle for 5600s (timeout 1800s)`
  - `last_activity=API call #21 completed`
  - `iteration=21/110`

That `5600s` matches the idle time since the previous turn, not the new turn.

## Root cause
Gateway caches `AIAgent` instances per session to preserve prompt caching. The inactivity watchdog asks the cached agent for `get_activity_summary()`, which reads `_last_activity_ts`.

`run_conversation()` did not reset `_last_activity_ts` early enough at the start of a fresh turn, so a reused agent could carry the previous turn's timestamp into the watchdog loop. If startup work before the first new API call takes a few seconds, the watchdog can classify the new turn as already timed out.

## Expected behavior
A fresh inbound message should reset activity immediately before any heavy per-turn setup work, so the watchdog measures inactivity for the current turn only.

## Proposed fix
At the start of `run_conversation()`, immediately call `_touch_activity("starting conversation turn")` and clear `self._current_tool` before provider checks, prompt assembly, memory prefetch, etc.

## Regression test
Added/should add a unit test asserting that a stale `_last_activity_ts` from a previous turn is reset before the first API call in a new `run_conversation()`.

[Feature]: Make delegate_task return durable task handles with lifecycle APIs and artifact references
items.body:
## Summary

Hermes `delegate_task` is already strong at spawning isolated subagents, parallel batch execution, heartbeat propagation, tool trace capture, and provider/toolset scoping.

A useful next step would be to borrow a pattern from **Relay Teams**: make delegated work return a **durable task handle** with explicit lifecycle operations and artifact references, instead of only returning a final inline JSON blob.

## Why this comparison came up

Today, Hermes `delegate_task` mainly behaves like:

- parent blocks until child / batch completes
- returns final JSON with `results[]`
- may print progress lines / spinner updates while running
- captures some metadata (`status`, `summary`, `api_calls`, `duration_seconds`, `tool_trace`, tokens, exit_reason)

That is already good for synchronous delegation.

But Relay Teams has a stronger pattern for long-running delegated work:

- start work -> get **task id / handle**
- observe with **list / wait / stop** primitives
- keep **logs / status / output paths** attached to that handle
- support **artifact-first workflows** (generated files, reports, PPTs, etc.)
- let the foreground agent continue doing other things while background work is still running

Hermes has some adjacent issues open around background delegation and `/tasks`, but I think there is still a missing core abstraction here: **delegation jobs as first-class runtime objects**.

## Current gap in Hermes

`delegate_task` returns the final result payload, but there is no built-in durable handle contract like:

- `task_id`
- `status` (`queued`, `running`, `completed`, `failed`, `cancelled`)
- `started_at` / `updated_at` / `completed_at`
- `child_session_id`
- `artifact_paths`
- `log_path`
- `wait_for_result(task_id)`
- `list_delegated_tasks()`
- `cancel_delegated_task(task_id)`

For short synchronous work, that's fine.
For longer-running or artifact-producing work, it becomes limiting.

## Why this would help

### 1) Better support for long-running delegated work

Not every delegated task should block the parent turn. Some work naturally wants to run in the background:

- repo-wide refactors
- research sweeps
- evaluation runs
- report generation
- file conversion / build pipelines

A durable handle makes these workflows much easier.

### 2) Stronger observability than transient progress text

Hermes already has spinner/progress behavior and some issues discussing `/tasks`, but progress text is ephemeral.
A task object with persistent state would let gateways / CLI / web UI all render the same source of truth.

### 3) Better artifact workflows

Relay Teams-style flows work well because tasks can produce concrete outputs and then hand back file paths / logs.
Hermes subagents already have isolated sessions and can clearly produce outputs, but `delegate_task` does not expose a standard artifact contract.

For example, a child could return:

```json
{
  "task_id": "deleg-123",
  "status": "completed",
  "summary": "Generated migration report",
  "artifact_paths": [
    "reports/migration_findings.md",
    "tmp/benchmarks/run_42.json"
  ],
  "log_path": "logs/deleg-123.log"
}
```

That would make delegation much more useful for real production workflows.

### 4) Cleaner parent-agent planning

If the parent can treat delegation as a managed runtime job, it can choose between:

- synchronous wait
- fire-and-forget
- poll until completion
- cancel on timeout
- aggregate multiple delegated jobs later

That is a more composable orchestration model.

## Suggested design direction

I think Hermes could introduce a small runtime layer for delegated jobs.

### Minimal version

Add a `background=true` / `return_handle=true` mode to `delegate_task` that returns immediately with:

- `task_id`
- `status`
- `child_session_ids`
- optional `expected_artifacts`

Then add companion primitives such as:

- `list_delegated_tasks`
- `wait_for_delegated_task`
- `cancel_delegated_task`
- `get_delegated_task_result`

### Result schema improvements

Even in synchronous mode, it would help to standardize richer result metadata:

- `task_id`
- `child_session_id`
- `status`
- `summary`
- `error`
- `tokens`
- `tool_trace`
- `artifact_paths`
- `log_path`
- `started_at` / `completed_at`

### Artifact contract

Allow subagents to explicitly surface generated outputs, not just natural-language summaries.
Possible forms:

- explicit return field from child runtime
- scan for declared output files in a working directory
- tool-level artifact registration during child execution

## Why I think this is not just a duplicate

There are already related issues open for:

- background delegation
- `/tasks`
- streaming / per-task completion delivery

But this proposal is a bit more foundational:

> treat delegated work as a **first-class managed job with durable handles and artifact references**, not just a blocking helper that returns final JSON.

That abstraction would make those other UX features easier to build consistently across CLI, gateway, web UI, and future orchestration layers.

## Concrete inspiration from Relay Teams

The Relay Teams pattern that seems most worth borrowing is:

1. **Task handle first**
2. **Lifecycle API** (`list/wait/stop`)
3. **Persistent observable state**
4. **Artifact-aware outputs**
5. **Decouple task execution from the parent turn**

Hermes already has a lot of the hard subagent machinery. This would mostly improve orchestration ergonomics and runtime observability.

## Code pointers

- `tools/delegate_tool.py`
  - `delegate_task()`
  - `_run_single_child()`
  - returned `results[]` schema
- related open issues:
  - background delegation
  - `/tasks`
  - per-task completion delivery

## Possible acceptance criteria

- A delegated task can optionally return immediately with a durable `task_id`
- Parent or UI can later inspect or wait on that `task_id`
- Delegated tasks expose persistent status and timestamps
- Delegated tasks can surface artifact paths / logs in a structured way
- Same abstraction works across CLI and gateway

items.title: [Feature]: Make delegate_task background mode reuse Hermes' existing background-task substrate
items.body:
## Summary

After comparing `delegate_task` with Hermes' **existing background task substrate**, I think the best improvement is **not** to invent a new delegation job system from scratch.

Instead, `delegate_task` should reuse / align with the background task primitives that Hermes already has:

- gateway `/background` execution via `_run_background_task()`
- CLI background task tracking
- `terminal(background=true)` process management
- `process` tool lifecycle APIs (`list / poll / log / wait / kill / write / submit / close`)
- background completion notifications / same-chat result delivery

In short:

> If Hermes wants non-blocking delegated work, the right direction is probably **delegate_task on top of the existing background task base**, not a separate parallel runtime with different semantics.

## Why I think this matters

Hermes already has two strong async foundations today:

### 1) Background agent tasks

The gateway `/background` flow already provides:

- task IDs
- non-blocking execution
- same-chat result delivery
- failure handling
- model/runtime resolution
- media / file extraction on completion
- tracked async tasks to avoid GC / dangling execution

Relevant code:

- `gateway/run.py`
  - `_handle_background_command()`
  - `_run_background_task()`

### 2) Background process management for long-running shell work

Hermes also already has a mature substrate for long-running processes started via:

- `terminal(background=true)`

with lifecycle operations exposed through:

- `process(action="list" | "poll" | "log" | "wait" | "kill" | ...)`

Relevant code:

- `tools/process_registry.py`
- `tools/terminal_tool.py`

So Hermes already solved much of the hard runtime / observability / lifecycle problem — just in adjacent layers.

## Current delegation gap

`delegate_task` is currently strong at:

- isolated child agents
- provider/toolset scoping
- parallel batch execution
- heartbeat propagation
- result metadata (`status`, `summary`, `api_calls`, `duration_seconds`, `tool_trace`, `tokens`, `exit_reason`)

But it is still mostly shaped like a **blocking helper**:

- spawn child agent(s)
- wait
- return final JSON blob inline

That works well for synchronous delegation.

What it does **not** yet cleanly inherit from the background task substrate is:

- durable background task identity aligned with the rest of Hermes
- unified lifecycle inspection / waiting / cancellation
- same abstraction for foreground, gateway, and future web UI
- structured artifact/log references using the same runtime model users already understand

## Why the solution should reuse existing substrate

If `delegate_task(background=true)` is introduced (or expanded), I think it should be implemented as a thin orchestration layer over the existing background task base.

That would avoid creating a third async model with its own:

- IDs
- status schema
- registries
- progress delivery semantics
- log handling rules
- cancellation flow

Hermes already seems to be moving in this direction conceptually: issue discussions around delegation background mode mention simplifying implementation by reusing `_run_background_task()` instead of maintaining a separate registry.

That feels like the right architectural instinct.

## Concrete proposal

### A. Add / formalize `delegate_task(background=true)` using the existing background task machinery

Instead of building a bespoke delegation runtime, background delegation should:

- create a normal Hermes background task ID
- execute the delegated child work through the existing background runner path
- reuse the same completion / failure delivery semantics as `/background`

### B. Return a handle that is compatible with existing background-task semantics

For example:

```json
{
  "task_id": "bg_142700_ab12cd",
  "status": "running",
  "kind": "delegation",
  "child_session_ids": ["ses_1", "ses_2"],
  "message": "Delegated tasks started in background"
}
```

The key point is: this should feel like a normal Hermes background task, not a new category with entirely different rules.

### C. Expose observability through already-familiar lifecycle APIs

If a delegated task runs in the background, users / agents should be able to inspect it the same way they inspect other async work:

- list active tasks
- wait for completion
- stop / cancel
- inspect output / logs

If there is already an internal background-task store, delegation should integrate with that instead of rolling its own.

### D. Reuse artifact and output delivery logic from `_run_background_task()`

One underrated benefit of the existing background substrate is that it already knows how to:

- extract media/files from responses
- deliver completion messages back to the originating chat
- preserve same-chat UX

Delegation should inherit that behavior rather than making artifact delivery a delegation-specific concern.

## Why this is better than the broader “new durable job system” framing

A previous version of this idea could be read as “please add a new managed delegation runtime with handles / lifecycle / artifacts”.

After reviewing the codebase more carefully, I think that framing is too broad and risks pushing Hermes toward duplicated infrastructure.

The better version is narrower and more aligned with the codebase:

> Extend `delegate_task` by **plugging into the existing background task substrate** and its observability model.

That gives most of the same benefits — task handles, non-blocking execution, better artifact delivery, unified UX — without splitting the architecture.

## Acceptance criteria

A good implementation would likely satisfy something like:

- `delegate_task(background=true)` starts non-blocking delegated work
- it returns a Hermes-style background `task_id`
- completion / failure is delivered via the same mechanisms as `/background`
- delegated background jobs are inspectable via the same task-observability model Hermes already uses
- artifact / media delivery reuses existing background task completion handling
- no separate bespoke delegation registry is required unless there is a proven gap in the shared substrate

## Code pointers

- `tools/delegate_tool.py`
  - `delegate_task()`
  - `_run_single_child()`
- `gateway/run.py`
  - `_handle_background_command()`
  - `_run_background_task()`
- `tools/process_registry.py`
  - existing lifecycle model for long-running async work
- `tools/terminal_tool.py`
  - `background=true`
- existing related issues / discussions around background delegation

## Closing thought

Hermes already has the beginnings of a coherent async runtime.

The opportunity here is not “add yet another async system for subagents”, but rather:

> make delegation a first-class user of the async substrate Hermes already trusts in production.

items.title: [Bug]: CLI status bar shows `ctx --` when LCM context engine is active — context_length never resolved
items.body:
### Bug Description

When `context.engine: lcm` is configured and hermes-lcm is the active context engine, the CLI status bar displays `ctx --` with an empty progress bar (`[░░░░░░░░░░]`) instead of the actual context fill percentage. The bar never shows meaningful data, even after the first API response.

```
⚕ minimax-m2.7 │ ctx -- │ [░░░░░░░░░░] -- │ 9m
```

## References

- `run_agent.py:~1306` — plugin engine initialization (fix location)
- `run_agent.py:~1550` — `switch_model` path (reference for correct pattern)
- `run_agent.py:~1340` — `on_session_start` call site with broken kwargs fallback
- `plugins/context_engine/lcm/engine.py` — LCMEngine (affected plugin)


### Steps to Reproduce

1. Install hermes-lcm into `~/.hermes/hermes-agent/plugins/context_engine/lcm/`
2. Configure `context.engine: lcm` in `~/.hermes/config.yaml`
3. Start a new Hermes CLI session: `hermes`
4. Observe the status bar — it shows `ctx --` with `[░░░░░░░░░░]` even after sending message

### Expected Behavior

Context size and usage updates after api calls
minimax-m2.7 │ 101K/204.8K │ [█████░░░░░] 50% │ 53m 


### Actual Behavior

**Status bar (broken):**
```
⚕ minimax-m2.7 │ ctx -- │ [░░░░░░░░░░] -- │ 9m
```

### Affected Component

CLI (interactive chat)

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

_No response_

### Operating System

Debian 13

### Python Version

3.13.5

### Hermes Version

latest

### Relevant Logs / Traceback

```shell

```

### Root Cause Analysis (optional)

In `run_agent.py`, the built-in `ContextCompressor` resolves `context_length` in its `__init__` by calling `get_model_context_length()`:

```python
# run_agent.py — built-in path (works correctly)
self.context_compressor = ContextCompressor(
    model=self.model,
    context_length=get_model_context_length(...),  # ← resolves here
    ...
)
```

However, external (plugin) context engines are instantiated via a different path that skips this:

```python
# run_agent.py — plugin engine path (broken)
_selected_engine = load_context_engine(engine_name)
self.context_compressor = _selected_engine  # ← no context_length set!
```

`on_session_start()` is called later with `context_length=getattr(self.context_compressor, "context_length", 0)` — but since `update_model` was never called on the plugin engine, `context_length` is 0. The status bar's calculation `context_tokens / context_length * 100` produces `0 / 0 = None` → `ctx --`.


### Proposed Fix (optional)

In `run_agent.py` (~line 1306), immediately after loading an external context engine, call `update_model()` with the resolved `context_length`:

```python
_selected_engine = load_context_engine(engine_name)
self.context_compressor = _selected_engine
if not self.quiet_mode:
    logger.info("Using context engine: %s", _selected_engine.name)

# FIX: Resolve context_length for external engines
from agent.model_metadata import get_model_context_length
_init_ctx_len = get_model_context_length(
    self.model,
    base_url=self.base_url,
    api_key=getattr(self, "api_key", ""),
    config_context_length=_config_context_length,
    provider=self.provider,
)
self.context_compressor.update_model(
    model=self.model,
    context_length=_init_ctx_len,
    base_url=self.base_url,
    api_key=getattr(self, "api_key", ""),
    provider=self.provider,
)
```

This mirrors what `switch_model` already does correctly. After the fix, the status bar shows the correct `context_length` from session start.

- Images from local absolute file paths
- Images sent by users in the chat

items.title: # [Bug]: Serial cron tick execution causes scheduled jobs to be silently skipped when preceding jobs run long
items.body:
## Description

When multiple cron jobs are due at overlapping times, `tick()` in `cron/scheduler.py` executes them **serially** in a `for` loop. If a preceding job takes several minutes (e.g., an AI agent session with multiple tool calls), subsequent jobs miss their grace window and are silently fast-forwarded by `get_due_jobs()` — they never execute.

This is a **silent data loss** issue: the user sees no error, no log entry saying "job X was skipped because job Y was still running." The job simply doesn't fire.

## Environment

- **Hermes Agent version**: 0.8.0
- **OS**: Ubuntu 22.04 (Linux)
- **Gateway mode**: systemd user service (`gateway run --replace`)
- **Number of cron jobs**: 5 (mix of interval and cron-expression schedules)

## Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure 3+ cron jobs with overlapping or adjacent schedules:
   - Job A: `*/5 * * * *` (every 5 min, runs 5-10 min per session)
   - Job B: `*/10 * * * *` (every 10 min, runs 3-5 min per session)
   - Job C: `15 8,10,12,14,16,18,20,22 * * *` (fixed times, runs 2-3 min)

2. Wait for a tick where Job A and Job B are both due before Job C's scheduled time.

3. Observe that Job A runs first (serial), then Job B runs second. By the time both complete, Job C's `next_run_at` is past its grace window.

4. On the next tick, `get_due_jobs()` detects Job C as stale and fast-forwards it to the next future run — **Job C never executes**.

## Root Cause Analysis

The issue is a chain of three design decisions that interact badly:

### 1. `tick()` executes jobs serially (scheduler.py L928-L964)

```python
# scheduler.py tick()
for job in due_jobs:
    advance_next_run(job["id"])
    # ... run_job(job) — this blocks until the entire AI agent session completes
    mark_job_run(job["id"], success, error)
    executed += 1
```

Each `run_job()` spawns a full `AIAgent` session that can take 1-15+ minutes. While it runs, no other job can execute.

### 2. File lock prevents overlapping ticks (scheduler.py L903-L915)

```python
lock_fd = open(_LOCK_FILE, "w")
fcntl.flock(lock_fd, fcntl.LOCK_EX | fcntl.LOCK_NB)
```

The 60-second ticker in `gateway/run.py` calls `tick()` every minute, but the `LOCK_NB` flag means if the previous tick is still running (blocked on a long job), the new tick is silently skipped. This is correct for preventing duplicate execution, but combined with serial execution it means **the entire scheduler is blocked**.

### 3. Stale grace window fast-forwards missed jobs (jobs.py L680-L700)

```python
grace = _compute_grace_seconds(schedule)
if kind in ("cron", "interval") and (now - next_run_dt).total_seconds() > grace:
    # Fast-forward to next future run — job is NOT executed
    new_next = compute_next_run(schedule, now.isoformat())
```

`_compute_grace_seconds()` uses `period // 2` clamped to [120s, 7200s]. For a job scheduled every 2 hours, grace = 1 hour. This is reasonable for gateway-restart scenarios, but **not** for the case where the scheduler itself is alive but blocked by other jobs.

### The deadly combination

```
Timeline (real example):
22:00:38  Job A starts (due at 22:00)
22:09:44  Job A finishes
22:10:44  Job A starts again (due at 22:10)
22:15:00  ← Job C should fire here, but tick() is blocked on Job A
22:20:56  Job A finishes
22:20:57  Job B starts (due at 22:20)
22:24:49  Job B finishes
22:37:33  Next tick finally picks up Job C
          → get_due_jobs() sees Job C is 22+ minutes late
          → grace for 2h-interval job = 3600s (1 hour)
          → 22 min < 1 hour, so it SHOULD still run...
          BUT: advance_next_run() was already called, or the tick
          state is inconsistent from the long blocking period
```

In practice, the job was skipped. The session file shows it was created at 22:37 instead of 22:15, and the expected output was never produced.

## Expected Behavior

All due jobs should execute regardless of how long other jobs take. A long-running Job A should not prevent Job C from firing at its scheduled time.

## Suggested Fix

### Option 1: Concurrent job execution (recommended)

Replace the serial `for` loop in `tick()` with concurrent execution using `threading.Thread` or `concurrent.futures.ThreadPoolExecutor`:

```python
from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor, as_completed

MAX_CONCURRENT_JOBS = 4  # configurable

def tick(verbose=True, adapters=None, loop=None):
    # ... acquire lock ...
    due_jobs = get_due_jobs()
    
    # Advance all next_run_at FIRST (at-most-once, under lock)
    for job in due_jobs:
        advance_next_run(job["id"])
    
    # Release lock, then execute concurrently
    # (each run_job() gets its own AIAgent session, already isolated)
    with ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=MAX_CONCURRENT_JOBS) as pool:
        futures = {
            pool.submit(_execute_single_job, job, adapters, loop): job
            for job in due_jobs
        }
        for future in as_completed(futures):
            job = futures[future]
            try:
                future.result()
            except Exception as e:
                logger.error("Job %s failed: %s", job["id"], e)
```

This is safe because:
- `run_job()` already creates an isolated `AIAgent` session per job
- Each job has its own session DB, environment variables, and output directory
- The file lock only needs to protect `get_due_jobs()` + `advance_next_run()`, not execution

### Option 2: Distinguish "scheduler-blocked" from "gateway-down" in grace logic

If concurrent execution is too risky, at minimum the grace logic should differentiate between:
- **Gateway was down** (restart scenario) → fast-forward is correct
- **Scheduler was busy** (serial blocking) → should still execute, just late

This could be done by recording a `last_tick_at` timestamp and checking if ticks were happening (scheduler alive but busy) vs. not happening (gateway down).

### Option 3: Add observability

Regardless of the execution model, when a job is fast-forwarded, emit a **warning-level** log and optionally notify the user:

```
WARNING: Job 'my-report' was skipped (scheduled 22:15, now 22:37, grace=3600s).
Reason: scheduler was blocked by other jobs for 22 minutes.
```

Currently the fast-forward log is INFO level and doesn't mention *why* the job was late, making debugging very difficult.

## Impact

- **Silent job skipping**: Users expect scheduled reports/tasks to run reliably. When they don't, there's no indication of what went wrong.
- **Unpredictable**: Which jobs get skipped depends on execution order and timing, making it hard to reproduce.
- **Workaround difficulty**: Users can't easily work around this without reducing the number of cron jobs or artificially shortening job execution times.

## Workaround

Currently the only workaround is to stagger cron schedules far apart (e.g., 30+ minute gaps) to ensure serial execution doesn't cause overlap. This defeats the purpose of having a scheduler.

items.body:
### Bug Description

Hermes has a discovery mismatch for third-party memory providers.

The general plugin docs and architecture say user plugins are discovered from ~/.hermes/plugins/, alongside project-local plugins and pip entry points. But the memory-provider developer docs describe providers as living under plugins/memory/<name>/, and issue #4956 says hermes memory setup and hermes memory status currently scan only the bundled source-tree plugins/memory/ directory.

### Steps to Reproduce

Reproduced this exactly with a third-party provider, Brainctl:

memory.provider: brainctl was set in config
plugin files existed under ~/.hermes/plugins/memory/brainctl
hermes memory status still reported Plugin: NOT installed
Hermes told us to install the plugin to ~/.hermes/plugins/
once the plugin was moved to ~/.hermes/plugins/brainctl and symlinked into ~/.hermes/hermes-agent/plugins/memory/brainctl, hermes memory status changed to installed and available

### Expected Behavior

memory provider installed correctly

### Actual Behavior

So the bug is that memory-provider discovery and related setup/status code are not aligned with the documented user plugin location. That matches the proposed fix in #4956: discover_memory_providers(), load_memory_provider(), and dependency resolution in memory_setup.py should also scan $HERMES_HOME/plugins/, with bundled providers taking precedence on name collisions.

Setup / Installation

## Feature Description

Add an automatic 'heartbeat' mechanism for long-running tasks. When an agent is actively processing a task for more than N seconds (e.g., 120s) without user interaction, it should proactively send a status update to notify the user that it hasn't hung.

## Motivation

When the agent is executing a long task (e.g., batch downloads, large file processing, multi-step workflows), the user has no way to know if the agent is still working or has hung. Currently:

- The user must wait passively or repeatedly ask 'are you still there?'
- There's no automatic notification if the task is genuinely stuck
- `terminal()` and `execute_code()` calls can run for minutes without any feedback

## Proposed Solution

Implement a lightweight watchdog that:
1. Activates automatically when a `terminal()` or `execute_code()` call exceeds a configurable timeout (default: 120s)
2. Sends a message to the user via the current messaging platform (Feishu/Telegram/etc.) saying '任务仍在运行中，已持续 X 分钟，请稍候...'
3. Can be dismissed or acknowledged by the user
4. Does NOT trigger if the task completes within the timeout

This could be implemented as:
- A background thread/timer in the agent that tracks active tool calls
- A per-session flag that gets set when a long-running tool starts
- The notification goes to the current conversation/session

## Alternatives Considered

- **Cron-based external watcher**: Requires separate process, complex setup, not session-aware
- **User manually enabling watchdog**: Works but requires user to remember to activate it each time
- **Periodic status messages regardless of task length**: Spams the user unnecessarily

## Additional Context

A reference implementation exists in Claude Code (the `--watchdog` flag or similar mechanism) which shows this pattern is well-received by users who run long tasks.

items.title: [Bug]: kimi-coding auxiliary calls fail with 400 "invalid temperature" when provider=auto
items.body:
### Bug Description

When `auxiliary.vision` or `auxiliary.session_search` is configured as `provider: auto` and the active main provider is `kimi-coding`, all auxiliary calls that pass a non-default temperature fail with a 400 error:

```
invalid temperature: only 1 is allowed for this model
```

The Kimi API (kimi-k2.5, kimi-k2-thinking, etc.) only accepts `temperature=1`. Both `vision_tools.py` and `session_search_tool.py` hardcode `temperature=0.1` in their `async_call_llm` calls. When `provider: auto` resolves to `kimi-coding` as the active provider, every affected auxiliary call silently returns a 400, breaking vision analysis and session summarisation.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Set `kimi-coding` as your main model (`hermes model kimi-coding/kimi-k2.5`)
2. Leave `auxiliary.vision` and `auxiliary.session_search` at their defaults (`provider: auto`)
3. Trigger a vision call (e.g. send an image in Discord/Telegram) **or** trigger session search
4. Observe 400 error in `~/.hermes/logs/errors.log`

Minimal config to reproduce:
```yaml
model:
  provider: kimi-coding
  default: kimi-k2.5
auxiliary:
  vision:
    provider: auto   # resolves to kimi-coding -> fails
  session_search:
    provider: auto   # resolves to kimi-coding -> fails
```

### Expected Behavior

Auxiliary calls to `kimi-coding` succeed. The temperature parameter is omitted for Kimi providers (letting the API use its default of 1), consistent with how the Codex adapter already strips unsupported parameters.

### Actual Behavior

`BadRequestError: Error code: 400` is raised on every auxiliary vision and session-search call:

```
openai.BadRequestError: Error code: 400 - invalid temperature: only 1 is allowed for this model
```

Vision analysis and session summarisation silently fail. The gateway continues running but those features are non-functional.

### Affected Component

Agent Core (conversation loop, context compression, memory), Tools (terminal, file ops, web, code execution, etc.)

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

Discord, Telegram

### Operating System

Ubuntu 24.04

### Python Version

3.11.15

### Hermes Version

0.8.0

### Relevant Logs / Traceback

```shell
2026-04-12 11:18:09,674 ERROR tools.vision_tools: Error analyzing image: Error code: 400 - invalid temperature: only 1 is allowed for this model

2026-04-13 10:20:45,466 WARNING root: Session summarization failed after 3 attempts: Error code: 400 - invalid temperature: only 1 is allowed for this model

Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "agent/auxiliary_client.py", line 2278, in async_call_llm
    return await client.chat.completions.create(**kwargs)
openai.BadRequestError: Error code: 400 - invalid temperature: only 1 is allowed for this model
```

### Root Cause Analysis (optional)

`_build_call_kwargs` in `agent/auxiliary_client.py` (line ~1955) unconditionally forwards the `temperature` kwarg to the API:

```python
if temperature is not None:
    kwargs["temperature"] = temperature   # sent to ALL providers, including kimi-coding
```

- `vision_tools.py:407` passes `"temperature": 0.1`
- `session_search_tool.py:161` passes `temperature=0.1`

The Codex adapter already strips unsupported parameters (see the comment at line 290: *"the Codex endpoint does NOT support max_output_tokens or temperature — omit to avoid 400 errors"*). The same treatment is needed for Kimi aliases (`kimi-coding`, `kimi`, `moonshot`).

### Proposed Fix (optional)

In `_build_call_kwargs`, skip `temperature` for Kimi provider aliases, mirroring the existing Codex pattern:

```python
if temperature is not None:
    # kimi-coding only accepts temperature=1; omit to use the API default.
    if provider not in {"kimi-coding", "kimi", "moonshot"}:
        kwargs["temperature"] = temperature
```

I am happy to submit a PR with this fix and accompanying regression tests.

Introduced by PR #2110 (commit `1055d435`) — the `not is_custom` guard skips `detect_provider_for_model()` when currently on a custom provider, which also prevents triple-suffix parsing. PR #2799 preserved this behavior during the refactor into `switch_model()`.

`parse_model_input()` in `hermes_cli/models.py` already has dedicated triple-suffix parsing logic (line 907), but `switch_model()` never calls it because the `is_custom` check short-circuits before reaching `detect_provider_for_model()`.

items.title: Bug: custom provider api_mode not passed to model validation, wrong catalog returned

labels.name: comp/cli
labels.description: CLI entry point, hermes_cli/, setup wizard

items.body:
## Problem

When switching to a named custom provider with `api_mode: anthropic_messages` (e.g. Claude Code Hub), the model validation step probes the `/models` endpoint without the `anthropic-version` header. The proxy returns the OpenAI model catalog instead of the Anthropic one, producing misleading warnings:

```
⚠ Note: `glm-5-turbo` was not found in this provider's model listing.
  Similar models: `gpt-5-pro`, `gpt-5.2-pro`
```

## Root Cause

Two issues in `hermes_cli/models.py`:

1. **`validate_requested_model()` doesn't accept `api_mode`** — `switch_model()` resolves `api_mode` from `resolve_runtime_provider()` (e.g. `"anthropic_messages"`) but never passes it to `validate_requested_model()`. The validation chain (`validate_requested_model` → `probe_api_models`) has no way to include the `anthropic-version` header.

2. **Named custom providers not recognized as custom** — `validate_requested_model()` checks `if normalized == "custom"`, but named custom providers like `custom:cch_anthropic` have `normalize_provider("custom:cch_anthropic")` → `"custom:cch_anthropic"`, which doesn't match. They fall through to the generic probe path (line ~1798) which also lacks `api_mode`.

3. **Generic fallback probe also missing `api_mode`** — Even if the custom check were fixed, the generic `fetch_api_models(api_key, base_url)` call at line ~1798 doesn't pass `api_mode` either.

## Reproduction

```yaml
# config.yaml
custom_providers:
  - name: cch_anthropic
    base_url: http://localhost:23000
    api_key: "${CCH_API_KEY}"
    api_mode: anthropic_messages
    models:
      glm-5-turbo:
        context_length: 202752
```

```
/model custom:cch_anthropic:glm-5-turbo
```

Expected: model validates against the Anthropic catalog.
Actual: validates against OpenAI catalog, warns about `gpt-5-pro` as similar model.

## Affected Code Path

```
switch_model() → validate_requested_model() → probe_api_models()
                                      ↘ fetch_api_models()
```

- `switch_model()` line ~622: resolves `api_mode` from runtime but drops it
- `validate_requested_model()` line ~1748: `if normalized == "custom"` misses `custom:*`
- `validate_requested_model()` line ~1798: `fetch_api_models(api_key, base_url)` — no `api_mode`
- `probe_api_models()` line ~1594: no `api_mode` param at all

items.title: [DingTalk] Add file/image sending support and fix 5 bugs in DingTalk adapter
items.body:
## Feature Description

Add file and image sending support to the DingTalk platform adapter (`gateway/platforms/dingtalk.py`).

Currently the adapter only supports sending markdown text replies via the session webhook. It should also support sending:
- Images (jpg, png, gif, bmp — up to 20MB)
- Files (doc, docx, xls, xlsx, ppt, pptx, zip, pdf, rar — up to 20MB)
- Voice messages (amr, mp3, wav — up to 2MB)

## Motivation

- Users want to receive generated documents, images, and other files from the agent through DingTalk
- The DingTalk API already supports these message types via session webhook
- The media upload permission (`/media/upload`) is **default-enabled** for enterprise internal apps — no additional permission needed
- Other platforms (Discord, Telegram) already support file sending

## Proposed Solution

1. **Upload flow**: Use DingTalk's `/media/upload` API to upload files and obtain `media_id`
2. **Send flow**: Send `image`/`file`/`voice` message types via session webhook (same endpoint, different `msgtype`)
3. **Integration**: Hook into the existing `send()` method or add a `send_file()` method

Session webhook already accepts these payloads:
```json
// Image
{"msgtype": "image", "image": {"media_id": "@xxx"}}

// File  
{"msgtype": "file", "file": {"media_id": "@xxx"}}
```

## Bugs Found During Setup

Also found 5 bugs in the current DingTalk adapter:

### Bug 1: `start()` should be `start_forever()`
`asyncio.to_thread(self._stream_client.start)` only gets a coroutine without executing it. The stream client exits immediately. Should use `start_forever()`.

### Bug 2: `process()` must be async
The SDK's `ChatbotHandler.process()` is an async method. The override must also be async, otherwise `raw_process` fails with `object tuple can't be used in 'await' expression`.

### Bug 3: `_extract_text()` wrong type handling
`message.text` is a `TextContent` object (has `.content` attr), not a dict or str. Current code produces garbled output like `TextContent(content=hello)` instead of extracting `hello`.

### Bug 4: `CallbackMessage` vs `ChatbotMessage`
The SDK passes `CallbackMessage` to `process()`, not `ChatbotMessage`. Need to extract from `CallbackMessage.data` via `ChatbotMessage.from_dict(data)`.

### Bug 5: Webhook URL regex too strict
`_DINGTALK_WEBHOOK_RE` only matches `api.dingtalk.com`, but session webhooks use `oapi.dingtalk.com`. Fix: `r'^https://(api|oapi)\.dingtalk\.com/'`

## Environment

- Hermes Agent (latest)
- DingTalk Stream Mode (dingtalk-stream SDK 0.24.3)
- Docker on Linux

### Bug Description

After running hermes gateway install --system --run-as-user root, the generated systemd service file sets ExecStart to the uv-managed Python binary instead of the venv Python. This bare uv Python has no packages installed, so the service crashes immediately on every start.

ExecStart=/root/.local/share/uv/python/cpython-3.11.15-linux-x86_64-gnu/bin/python3.11

Should be:

ExecStart=/root/.hermes/hermes-agent/venv/bin/python3.11

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Install Hermes on a fresh Ubuntu 24.04 VPS using the one-line installer
2. Run hermes gateway setup and configure Telegram
3. Run hermes gateway install --system --run-as-user root
4. Run systemctl start hermes-gateway
5. Check logs:

journalctl -u hermes-gateway -n 20

6. Confirm wrong Python path in service file:

cat /etc/systemd/system/hermes-gateway.service | grep ExecStart

### Expected Behavior

ExecStart points to the venv Python at /root/.hermes/hermes-agent/venv/bin/python3.11 where all packages are installed. Service starts successfully.

### Actual Behavior

ExecStart points to /root/.local/share/uv/python/cpython-3.11.15-linux-x86_64-gnu/bin/python3.11 — the raw uv-managed Python with no packages installed. Service crashes immediately with:

ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'yaml'
  File "/root/.hermes/hermes-agent/utils.py", line 10, in <module>
    import yaml

### Affected Component

Gateway (Telegram/Discord/Slack/WhatsApp)

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

N/A (CLI only), Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp

### Operating System

Ubuntu 24.04 LTS

### Python Version

3.11.15

### Hermes Version

v0.8.0

### Relevant Logs / Traceback

```shell
ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'yaml'
  File "/root/.hermes/hermes-agent/utils.py", line 10, in <module>
    import yaml
```

### Root Cause Analysis (optional)

The service file generator likely uses sys.executable to determine the Python path when writing ExecStart. When uv manages Python, sys.executable returns the underlying uv Python path rather than the venv Python. See [uv issue #11048](https://github.com/astral-sh/uv/issues/11048) for the upstream behavior.

### Proposed Fix (optional)

When generating the systemd unit file, resolve the Python path from VIRTUAL_ENV/bin/python3.11 rather than sys.executable. The venv path is already correctly set in the VIRTUAL_ENV environment variable written to the same service file.

items.title: [Feature]: ignored_threads config for Telegram topic filtering
items.body:
### Problem or Use Case

When running multiple bot profiles in the same Telegram supergroup (each in its own forum topic), there's no way to tell a bot to **ignore** messages from specific topics at the gateway level.

Currently:
- `group_topics` only handles **skill binding** — it maps topics to skills but doesn't act as a whitelist
- A bot configured for Topic A still receives messages from Topic B if mentioned or if `require_mention` is off
- The only workaround is SOUL.md instructions ("ignore this topic"), but the model still generates a response (e.g., "not responding to this topic") — wasting an LLM call and sending unwanted messages


### Proposed Solution


Add an `ignored_threads` list to the Telegram platform `extra` config. Messages from these thread IDs get silently dropped in `_should_process_message` before any processing.

 Config

```yaml
platforms:
  telegram:
    extra:
      ignored_threads:
        - 31    # Ace bot's topic — this bot should never respond here
        - 42    # Another topic to ignore
```

Code Change (6 lines in `_should_process_message`)

```python
# After the group chat check, before free_response_chats check:
thread_id = getattr(message, "message_thread_id", None)
if thread_id is not None:
    ignored = self.config.extra.get("ignored_threads", [])
    if int(thread_id) in [int(t) for t in ignored]:
        return False
```

Why This Matters

- **Zero LLM cost** — message is dropped before reaching the agent
- **Zero noise** — no "not responding" messages in the wrong topic
- **Config-driven** — no code changes needed per bot, just update config.yaml
- **Multi-bot friendly** — essential for setups where multiple bots share one supergroup with forum topics

## Current Workaround

Running this as a local patch with a post-merge git hook to reapply after updates. Works fine but would be much better as a native feature.


### Alternatives Considered

_No response_

### Feature Type

Gateway / messaging improvement

### Scope

Small (single file, < 50 lines)

items.title: Plugin context engines missing context_length — status bar shows ctx --
items.body:
## Problem

When a plugin context engine (e.g. hermes-lcm) is active, the CLI status bar shows `ctx --` with an empty progress bar because `context_length` is never resolved for external engines.

## Root Cause

The built-in `ContextCompressor` gets `context_length` via `get_model_context_length()` in its init path. Plugin context engines loaded via `load_context_engine()` skip this — `update_model()` is never called, so `context_length` stays at 0.

`on_session_start()` later reads `context_length=getattr(self.context_compressor, "context_length", 0)` which is 0, and the status bar calculation `context_tokens / context_length * 100` produces `None` → `ctx --`.

## Suggested Fix

In `run_agent.py` (~line 1306), after loading an external context engine, call `update_model()`:

```python
_selected_engine = load_context_engine(engine_name)
self.context_compressor = _selected_engine

from agent.model_metadata import get_model_context_length
_init_ctx_len = get_model_context_length(
    self.model,
    base_url=self.base_url,
    api_key=getattr(self, "api_key", ""),
    config_context_length=_config_context_length,
    provider=self.provider,
)
self.context_compressor.update_model(
    model=self.model,
    context_length=_init_ctx_len,
    base_url=self.base_url,
    api_key=getattr(self, "api_key", ""),
    provider=self.provider,
)
```

This mirrors what `switch_model` already does correctly (~line 1550).

## Impact

Low severity — functional behavior is unaffected, only the status bar display is broken for plugin context engines.

## References

Originally reported as stephenschoettler/hermes-lcm#12 by @strueman with full diagnosis.

items.title: [Bug]: Anthropic fast mode passes speed as unsupported top-level SDK kwarg
items.body:
## Bug Description
Anthropic fast mode for native Opus models currently stores `speed="fast"` as a top-level kwarg in `build_anthropic_kwargs()`. That kwargs dict is later unpacked into `self._anthropic_client.messages.stream(**api_kwargs)` and `messages.create(**api_kwargs)`, but recent Anthropic Python SDKs do not accept `speed` as a named argument. The result is an immediate non-retryable client error instead of a fast-mode response.

Observed failure:

```shell
ERROR root: Non-retryable client error: Messages.stream() got an unexpected keyword argument 'speed'
```

## Steps to Reproduce
1. Configure Hermes to use native Anthropic Opus 4.6 (`claude-opus-4-6` / `anthropic/claude-opus-4.6`).
2. Enable fast mode with `/fast fast`.
3. Send the next user message on the same session.
4. Hermes resolves the fast-mode override to `{"speed": "fast"}` and calls the Anthropic Messages streaming path.
5. The SDK raises `Messages.stream() got an unexpected keyword argument 'speed'`.

## Expected Behavior
Fast mode should remain enabled for supported native Anthropic models, but the request should be shaped in a way the Anthropic SDK accepts. Hermes should stream or create successfully while still sending the fast-mode beta request payload.

## Actual Behavior
Hermes crashes the request immediately because `speed` is passed as a top-level kwarg to the SDK instead of being nested under `extra_body`.

## Affected Component
- Gateway (Telegram/Discord/Slack/WhatsApp)
- Agent Core (conversation loop, context compression, memory)

## Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)
- Discord

## Operating System
macOS (observed from a local reproduction)

## Python Version
3.13.7 locally in the current dev environment

## Hermes Version
Current `main` as of April 13, 2026 (exact local checkout SHA available if needed)

## Relevant Logs / Traceback
```shell
ERROR root: Non-retryable client error: Messages.stream() got an unexpected keyword argument 'speed'
```

## Root Cause Analysis (optional)
`agent/anthropic_adapter.py` currently sets `kwargs["speed"] = "fast"` in `build_anthropic_kwargs()`. Those kwargs are later unpacked directly into Anthropic SDK calls in `run_agent.py`, including the streaming path. The Anthropic SDK supports arbitrary provider-specific payload extensions through `extra_body`, but not a top-level `speed` kwarg here.

The existing adapter tests in `tests/cli/test_fast_command.py` also assert the wrong contract today by expecting `kwargs["speed"] == "fast"`.

## Proposed Fix (optional)
Store the fast-mode parameter under `kwargs.setdefault("extra_body", {})["speed"] = "fast"` while preserving the existing fast-mode beta header injection. Update the fast-mode tests to assert that `speed` lives only under `extra_body` and is not forwarded as a top-level SDK kwarg.

- Hermes sends the success message:
  `Home channel set to ...`
- later, after restart / redeploy, Hermes again sends:
  `No home channel is set for Whatsapp`
- new WhatsApp users keep receiving the setup prompt even though an admin chat
  had already run `/sethome`

While debugging this, WhatsApp home-channel handling appeared to be inconsistent with other platforms:

- `/sethome` writes `WHATSAPP_HOME_CHANNEL=<chat_id>` into `~/.hermes/config.yaml`
- the startup warning path checks `os.getenv("WHATSAPP_HOME_CHANNEL")`
- `gateway/config.py` applies env home-channel overrides for Telegram, Discord,
  Slack, Signal, Mattermost, etc., but not for WhatsApp

This makes WhatsApp home-channel persistence look fragile and not fully aligned with the rest of the Gateway home-channel model.

### Steps to Reproduce

1. Configure Hermes with WhatsApp enabled in bot mode.
2. Start Hermes Gateway.
3. From an admin/personal WhatsApp chat, send a message to the bot.
4. In that same chat, run `/sethome`.
5. Observe the success message confirming the home channel was set.
6. Restart Hermes or redeploy the Hermes container/image.
7. Send a message from a new WhatsApp user/chat.

### Expected Behavior

- Once `/sethome` succeeds, the WhatsApp home channel should persist across
  normal restart / redeploy.
- New WhatsApp users should not be told that no WhatsApp home channel is set.
- WhatsApp should behave consistently with other platforms that support home
  channels.


### Actual Behavior

- `/sethome` reports success in the moment.
- After restart / redeploy, Hermes behaves as if no WhatsApp home channel is set.
- New WhatsApp users still receive the:
  `No home channel is set for Whatsapp`
  onboarding-style warning.


### Affected Component

Gateway (Telegram/Discord/Slack/WhatsApp)

### Messaging Platform (if gateway-related)

WhatsApp

### Operating System

Linux (Docker Compose deployment)

### Python Version

Python 3.13

### Hermes Version

v0.8.0 (2026.4.8)

### Relevant Logs / Traceback

```shell
Observed user-facing messages:


✅ Home channel set to <MyName> (ID: 54449219494114@lid).
Cron jobs and cross-platform messages will be delivered here.


Later, after restart / redeploy:


📬 No home channel is set for Whatsapp. A home channel is where Hermes delivers cron job results and cross-platform messages.

Type /sethome to make this chat your home channel, or ignore to skip.


Relevant code paths observed while debugging:

- `gateway/run.py`
  - `_handle_set_home_command`
  - first-message “no home channel set” prompt
- `gateway/config.py`
  - env home-channel overrides exist for multiple platforms, but WhatsApp does
    not appear to receive equivalent `WHATSAPP_HOME_CHANNEL` handling
```

### Root Cause Analysis (optional)

Based on code inspection, the issue appears to come from an inconsistency between how WhatsApp home-channel state is written and how it is reloaded:

- `/sethome` writes `WHATSAPP_HOME_CHANNEL=<chat_id>` into `~/.hermes/config.yaml`
- the first-message onboarding/warning logic checks whether
  `os.getenv("WHATSAPP_HOME_CHANNEL")` is set
- `gateway/config.py` applies home-channel env overrides for several platforms
  (Telegram, Discord, Slack, Signal, Mattermost, etc.), but not for WhatsApp

That makes WhatsApp different from the other platforms in two ways:

1. The persisted home-channel value is not clearly reloaded into the same path used by the warning logic.
2. WhatsApp does not appear to have the same env/config parity that other home-channel-capable platforms have.

So the likely result is:

- `/sethome` works immediately in the current process
- but after restart / redeploy, Hermes can fall back into a state where the WhatsApp home channel is no longer recognized as configured


### Proposed Fix (optional)

One possible fix would be to make WhatsApp home-channel loading consistent with the existing platform pattern:

1. In `gateway/config.py`, add WhatsApp home-channel env override handling similar to the existing Telegram / Signal / Discord logic, for example by honoring:
   - `WHATSAPP_HOME_CHANNEL`
   - optionally `WHATSAPP_HOME_CHANNEL_NAME`

2. Ensure `/sethome` persists WhatsApp home-channel state in the same shape that startup expects, so that restart/redeploy does not lose the effective value.

3. Make the “no home channel set” prompt rely on the fully loaded Gateway config instead of only checking `os.getenv(...)`, so persisted config and env overrides behave consistently.

4. Add a regression test covering:
   - WhatsApp `/sethome`
   - gateway restart / config reload
   - no repeat “No home channel is set for Whatsapp” prompt after restart

---
name: feat-compress-ui-blocking
about: Show progress UI and block input during /compress
title: "feat: /compress should show progress UI and block input during compression"
labels: enhancement
---

## Problem

`/compress` runs synchronously on the main thread with no visual feedback. For large sessions (400K+ tokens), the auxiliary LLM call to summarize middle turns can take 60-120 seconds. During this time:

1. No progress indicator — user sees only "🗜️ Compressing..." and then nothing
2. Input not blocked — user can type while compression is running
3. No `_invalidate()` calls — TUI doesn't repaint, spinner/activity feed doesn't update
4. Silent hangs — if the auxiliary model call fails/times out, user has no idea

This is especially bad with the default `ContextCompressor` which tries to summarize ALL middle turns in one massive LLM call.

## Proposed Fix

Similar to how `_clarify_callback`, `_sudo_password_callback`, and `_approval_callback` work:

1. Set a compression state flag (`self._compressing = True`)
2. Block input area via `Condition` filter on input keybindings
3. Show a spinner/progress message in status bar or below input
4. Call `_invalidate()` periodically during compression
5. Clear state on completion/failure

## Alternative: Background thread

For a more robust solution, run compression in a background thread and call `_invalidate()` every 2 seconds to show a spinning indicator.

## Impact

- User sees clear progress during compression (no "is it hanging?" uncertainty)
- Input is blocked so user can't accidentally type during compression
- TUI stays responsive (spinner updates)
- Consistent with other long-running callbacks (clarify, sudo, approval)

items.title: WhatsApp adapter missing send_voice() override — voice messages sent as text path

labels.name: P1
labels.description: High — major feature broken, no workaround

labels.name: sweeper:implemented-on-main
labels.description: Sweeper: behavior already present on current main

items.body:
## Problem

The WhatsApp platform adapter does not have a \`send_voice()\` override, causing voice/audio messages to fall back to the base class implementation which sends them as plain text (e.g., \`🔊 Audio: /path/to/file.mp3\`) instead of native media attachments.

## Root Cause

\`gateway/platforms/whatsapp.py\` has overrides for \`send_image\`, \`send_image_file\`, \`send_video\`, and \`send_document\` — but no \`send_voice\`. When the base class (\`gateway/platforms/base.py\`) calls \`self.send_voice()\`, it falls back to the default implementation at line ~1113 which just returns a text string.

This affects two separate paths:

1. **Auto-TTS path** — user sends a voice message → base.py calls \`self.play_tts()\` → calls \`self.send_voice()\` → no override → text fallback
2. **Explicit TTS tool path** — model calls \`text_to_speech\` tool → \`run.py\` extracts \`MEDIA:\` tag from tool result → \`extract_media()\` routes to \`self.send_voice()\` → same fallback

Every other platform adapter (Telegram, Discord, Signal, Slack, Matrix, BlueBubbles, WeCom, Weixin, Mattermost, Feishu) has this override. WhatsApp is the only one missing it.

## Fix

Add \`send_voice()\` method to \`gateway/platforms/whatsapp.py\`:

\`\`\`python
async def send_voice(
    self,
    chat_id: str,
    audio_path: str,
    caption: Optional[str] = None,
    reply_to: Optional[str] = None,
    **kwargs,
) -> SendResult:
    """Send audio file as native media via bridge."""
    return await self._send_media_to_bridge(chat_id, audio_path, "audio", caption)
\`\`\`

This routes through the existing \`_send_media_to_bridge()\` method with \`media_type="audio"\`. The bridge (\`bridge.js\` line ~468-471) already handles \`"audio"\` type — it reads the file and sends \`sock.sendMessage({ audio: buffer, mimetype: "audio/mpeg" })\`.

## Note

The bridge sends \`.mp3\` files as regular audio attachments (music player style). Voice note bubbles (PTT) are only sent for \`.ogg\` or \`.opus\` extensions. This is correct WhatsApp behavior, not a bug — if voice bubbles are desired for TTS, the adapter would need to either convert to \`.ogg\` or add \`ptt: true\` to the bridge audio payload.
